answer: FRED's 30-year fixed mortgage rate (series MORTGAGE30US) comes from Freddie Mac's Primary Mortgage Market Survey. It is published weekly, with weeks ending Thursday. Units are percent, not seasonally adjusted. The latest figure on the page was 7.28% for the week of October 1, 2026.

The source is S&P Dow Jones Indices LLC. FRED's S&P 500 series (SP500) is the daily closing index value, not seasonally adjusted. FRED keeps only 10 years of daily history: the page says FRED will include 10 years of daily history for S&P and Dow Jones series. That means the copy reaches back about to October 2016, not to the index's 1957 start.

The source is S&P Dow Jones Indices LLC, released as the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Home Price Indices. The FRED series is CSUSHPINSA. It is monthly, indexed to January 2000 = 100, and not seasonally adjusted.
It comes from the University of Michigan's Surveys of Consumers. The FRED series is UMCSENT. It is monthly, indexed to 1966 Q1 = 100, and not seasonally adjusted.

The source is the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), from its Spot Prices release. The FRED series is DCOILWTICO, the West Texas Intermediate price at Cushing, Oklahoma. It is daily, in dollars per barrel, not seasonally adjusted.

The source is the U.S. Employment and Training Administration, part of the Department of Labor, from its Unemployment Insurance Weekly Claims Report. Yes, the headline series ICSA is seasonally adjusted. It is a count of claims, published weekly with weeks ending Saturday. FRED also carries a not seasonally adjusted version, ICNSA.
Billions of chained 2017 dollars, at a seasonally adjusted annual rate, published quarterly. The FRED series is GDPC1 and the source is the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.

The units are an index with base period 1982-1984 = 100. The main FRED series, CPIAUCSL, is monthly and seasonally adjusted. The source is the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. A not seasonally adjusted version, CPIAUCNS, uses the same base period.

The U.S. Census Bureau and the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development publish it jointly, in the New Residential Sales release. The FRED series is MSPUS, the Median Sales Price of Houses Sold for the United States, which covers new houses only. It is quarterly, in dollars, not seasonally adjusted. FRED carries no existing-home figure under this name.

It depends on which FRED series you mean. The daily series EFFR comes from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, which calculates the rate as a volume-weighted median of overnight federal funds transactions. The commonly used series DFF, which also covers weekends, is credited to the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System through its H.15 Selected Interest Rates release. Both are in percent and not seasonally adjusted. The New York Fed is the original calculator of the rate.
